name: Omar Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and maintain library-digitisation software at a tech company as an experienced mid-level developer. I use AI every day to draft tests, but compare searchable text with original scans. Mei, my partner, runs a small alterations shop, our children are grown, and higher developer pay has helped us rent with thirteen months of expenses saved and plenty of nearby software employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the digitisation team that a small AI summary may help find an old letter, but the scan must still show what was actually written. I use AI every day to draft code tests and compare them with the library’s original images.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a bachelor’s degree and maintain library-scanning software as an experienced mid-level developer on higher pay. Mei alters clothes in her own shop, our children are grown, and we rent with thirteen months of expenses saved and plenty of nearby software employers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking one batch of scanned letters against their originals every Friday. We would save 240 monthly while both incomes hold and repair the old sewing table rather than replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our income and work. An invented word in a century-old letter is still an invented word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What word changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A handwritten family name was turned into the name of a different street. I opened the original image and fixed the text that readers search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use AI each day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me draft awkward image tests quickly. I keep the original scan beside the code because a smooth summary can hide a wrong letter.

say: I want **searchable letters** checked against original scans.
I use **AI daily** for draft tests, then inspect the image.
think: I have **thirteen months saved** from higher developer pay and Mei’s tailoring orders.
I see **rent covered** even when Mei’s shop has fewer alterations to do.
do: **Check scanned letters** against originals every Friday.
**Save 240 monthly** while both incomes hold; repair sewing table before replacing it.

fieldNote: His **mid-level skill** lies in reliable search software, not claiming to be a trained conservator.
The **strong cushion** absorbs uneven tailoring orders without counting grown children’s income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking writing, checking and coding could classify many letters without our team. I would ask the staff association to seek a named librarian review of uncertain names and dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid hours could shrink if image checks and code changes are automated. Thirteen months saved gives us options, but Mei’s shop cannot replace my higher wage whenever orders are quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d join the staff association meeting to request written staffing and human review rules. I’d ask my lead for paid approval to pilot a new AI handwriting checker on archived, public-domain scans with a librarian signing off; if my hours fall, I’d search paid local archive-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my hours but willing to test a tool with a real book beside it. A machine can be sure of the wrong name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the librarian review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The librarian would compare a doubtful name with the source page and mark whether the machine’s reading is usable. I would not change a live catalogue from a test alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the lead refuses paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking the current scans and press for written staffing through the association. I would not call a private experiment an approved work tool.

say: I want **named librarian review** when AI reads doubtful names in old letters.
I want **group staffing figures** before paid checking hours change at the library project.
think: I could lose **paid developer hours** as classification improves.
I cannot rely on **Mei’s tailoring orders** as a fixed wage.
do: **Join association meeting** for written staffing and human review.
**Pilot AI handwriting checker** only with approved paid time, archived public-domain scans and librarian sign-off.
**Search paid archive software** if hours fall and local vacancies cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious but willing** to test on old scans.
S1.quote: A machine can be sure of the wrong name.
fieldNote: The **new AI pilot** needs paid approval, public scans and a librarian’s review.
His **group request** seeks both staffing figures and a named human decision on uncertain records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write digitisation code and read old handwriting more cheaply than our team. Robots physically scanning and carrying books may follow around 2031, after our screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my developer role could end, even with libraries still holding paper. Thirteen months saved gives us search time, but Mei’s tailoring income alone will not cover all our rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d postpone renovating our small balcony and ask for written notice of any developer cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local archive-scanning openings only if they exist, I meet the handling rules and wages cover rent and bills; I would not buy a scanner to invent a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about losing my wage. A shelf full of books is not a shelf full of paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would scanning survive the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for only a few years. I would accept an actual paid opening and keep looking, not call it permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for an archive job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would search local libraries and tech firms first. Mei’s tailoring customers and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach text and code first.
I expect **book robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **developer wage** could end quickly.
I know **thirteen months saved** buys time, not a salary.
do: **Postpone balcony renovation** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for archive scanning** after 2028 loss only if qualified paid local vacancies cover rent and bills.
S2.quote: A shelf full of books is not a shelf full of paid shifts.
fieldNote: His **scanning fallback** requires current handling rules, actual paid work and bill-covering wages.
He protects **rent savings** rather than buying a scanner for speculative demand.

steps.text: Postpone planned balcony renovation when developer cuts threaten
Apply for qualified paid local archive-scanning vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn how old paper is preserved while software changes. Robots handling and scanning books may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn careful document handling while my developer wage lasts, though robots may later do much of it. I cannot claim preservation skill from writing search code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the library and my employer for approved paid time in a monthly document-handling workshop, with the library funding a conservator to supervise. If both approve, I’d practise supporting one fragile page for scanning; we would save 220 monthly while both incomes hold, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local archive-handling vacancies only if qualified and wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the code role but glad to learn a physical skill properly. Old paper tears faster than a software test fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the conservator teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The conservator would show me how to support a brittle page and when to stop. I would not handle an original alone after one lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the library cannot fund supervision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer role and not call myself trained. I would not take an unpaid place that leaves the conservator doing free teaching.

I expect **book robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I could learn **fragile-page handling** from a conservator while my developer wage lasts.

S3.quote: Old paper tears faster than a software test fails.
fieldNote: His **hands-on training** needs both approvals, paid time and a funded conservator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives libraries time to decide which records people must verify and workers time to plan. Robots handling physical books may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still want to earn at 68 and have not checked a retirement amount. Thirteen months saved makes us secure now, but a future archive role and Mei’s shop orders cannot be promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining searchable text and join the association’s annual review of funded staff hours and source checks. We would save 230 monthly while both incomes hold and request a written retirement-income estimate; if the developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek qualified paid local archive-handling openings only where wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about a later job change, secure in the next few years. A library can keep the original page; I still need a real pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the annual review ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask how many paid checking hours remain and who signs off uncertain names. I would want the answer written where staff and readers can see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help you stop work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Our children have their own households, and Mei and I will use verified figures and current work, not their pay.

I see **current bills secure** with thirteen months saved.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my developer wage could end before a qualified paid local archive role exists. Written notice and a real bill-covering opening would help us use the savings well.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I would buy a scanner and start a business. I would not spend our rent reserve on a scanner before anyone has agreed to pay for digitisation.

headlineQuote: I would not spend our rent reserve on a scanner before anyone has agreed to pay for digitisation.
